query: For Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state, the factors governing its phase stability during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure are not understood well enough to account for the range of phases that may appear. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain this behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations relative to that baseline, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: During cooling and subsequent thermal exposure, local chemical short‐range order (SRO) develops driven by differential atomic stresses—especially the negative local stress of Cr atoms—which leads to the nucleation of additional phases from the high-temperature BCC state. In other words, varying cooling rates allow or hinder the formation of Cr-rich clusters that mediate phase transformation.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in a high-temperature BCC state
generation.intervention: Apply controlled cooling protocols (fast quenching vs. slow cooling) followed by defined thermal annealing steps.
generation.conditions: The test applies during thermal paths that allow sufficient atomic mobility (i.e., slow cooling or post-cooling annealing at moderate temperatures below the BCC stability range). It should not apply, or be greatly diminished, when the cooling is rapid enough to suppress atomic rearrangements (quenching) or in systems with significantly altered grain sizes (e.g., nanoscale dimensions where diffusion is constrained).
generation.structural_mediator: Locally enhanced chemical short-range order due to Cr atoms developing negative atomic stress, which, in combination with the positive stresses from Co, Fe, Ni, and Al, creates local compositional fluctuations.
generation.mechanism: During controlled slow cooling or thermal exposure, Cr atoms tend to segregate into clusters because of their inherent negative atomic stress. This segregation establishes localized SRO, altering the nucleation kinetics and promoting the formation of secondary phases (e.g., FCC or possible intermetallic phases) compared to the metastable BCC baseline. In contrast, rapid quenching prevents sufficient atomic diffusion and SRO establishment, retaining the uniform BCC state.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples subjected to slow cooling or subsequent annealing should display additional phases and microstructural evidence of Cr-rich clusters (as revealed by techniques such as XRD, TEM, or atom probe tomography), whereas rapidly quenched samples will predominantly retain the single-phase BCC structure with minimal SRO.
generation.baseline: Rapidly quenched Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 from the high-temperature BCC state, maintaining a uniform elemental distribution with little to no short-range ordering.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected when sufficient atomic mobility is available (i.e., in samples with grain sizes and thermal histories that permit diffusion). It may not apply in ultrafast quenching, where diffusion is severely suppressed, or in alloy compositions where Cr concentration or its stress characteristics are significantly different.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative impact of Cr-induced stress on phase separation kinetics is uncertain, and the details of the secondary phase structures (e.g., exact crystal structures) may vary with subtle changes in processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples from the same high-temperature BCC state. One set is rapidly quenched to freeze the high-temperature state, and the other is slowly cooled followed by controlled annealing. Characterize microstructures and phase compositions using X-ray diffraction (XRD), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and atom probe tomography (APT) to assess chemical short-range order and phase evolution.
measurements: XRD to detect the presence and relative amounts of different phases
TEM for microstructural and phase boundary observations
APT/EDS for mapping local elemental distributions and identifying Cr-rich clusters
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the slowly cooled/annealed samples do not exhibit statistically significant differences (e.g., the appearance of additional phases or detectable Cr-rich SRO) compared to the rapidly quenched baseline, then the hypothesis that Cr-induced SRO drives additional phase transformations will be falsified.

## Abstract
The issue of elemental distribution such as chemical short range order (SRO) in high entropy alloys (HEAs) has garnered increased attention in both experimental and theoretical realms. A comprehensive and urgently required elucidation of this atomic-level phenomenon is the focus of this study. In this work, we systematically analyzed atomic-level information, involving atomic volume, charge transfer, local chemical ordering and atomic stress in 3d HEAs. We assess the hotly debated issue by attributing it to Cr atoms with negative atomic stress in the sublattice site, whereas other atoms with positive atomic stress have larger electronegativity and greater atomic volume, through which the interplay of positive and negative atomic stresses balances the local atomic environment. Additionally, we assume that Mn promotes the homogeneity of the HEA and the temperature-dependent chemical SRO enhances the thermal stability of HEAs. Our work contributes to advancing our understanding of the mechanistic aspects of elemental distribution in HEAs and their thermodynamic implications. ## Abstract
This study investigates the influence of cooling rates on the microstructure and phase transformations of the high-entropy alloy Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20. The alloy was synthesized via arc melting and subjected to three cooling conditions: slow cooling (52 K/s), accelerated cooling after a short electric arc pulse (3018 K/s), and rapid quenching (10⁵–10⁶ K/s) using the melt-spinning method. The microstructures were characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and Mössbauer spectroscopy. The thermal properties and phase transformations were analyzed using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and thermography. Slow cooling produced a complex crystalline microstructure, while accelerated cooling resulted in fewer phases. Rapid cooling yielded an amorphous structure, demonstrating that phosphorus and high mixing entropy enhance glass-forming ability. Phase transformations exhibited significant undercooling under accelerated cooling, with FCC phase crystallization shifting from 1706 K (slow cooling) to 1341 K, and eutectic crystallization from 1206 K to 960 K.
